lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Rebase a branch without conflicts
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `git init`, commit a file on main, run `git switch -c feature` and commit a change to a different file, then `git switch main` and commit a change to another file. Run `git switch feature` and `git rebase main`, then confirm with `git log --oneline --graph` that the history is linear with no merge commit.

explanations.topic: Rebasing brings main's commits into the feature branch without a merge commit
Feature commits are set aside and reapplied on top of main's latest commit
Why it's called rebasing: new base commit

hints: Make sure the feature branch and main each change a different file, so the rebase won't conflict.
Before running the rebase, switch to the feature branch. Run it from feature, not from main.
Run `git rebase main` while on feature, then `git log --oneline --graph`. Every line should be a single `*` with no branching lines.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while still on main, which does nothing.
Editing the same file on both branches, which causes a conflict in this step.
Forgetting to commit on main after switching back, so there's nothing to rebase onto.
Using `git merge main` instead, which creates a merge commit.
steps.code:
git init
git add . && git commit -m "initial commit"
git switch -c feature
# edit a different file
git commit -am "feature change"
git switch main
# edit another file
git commit -am "main change"
git switch feature
git rebase main
git log --oneline --graph

steps.title: Check whether the branch was pushed
steps.instructions: Run `git branch -a` to list local and remote branches. Only rebase if your feature branch does not appear under `remotes/`.

targets.caption: The asterisk marks your current local branch.
Remote-tracking branches; your feature branch must not be here.

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so they no longer match the remote
Why merge is safe: it doesn't rewrite history
Using git branch -a to see whether the feature branch was pushed

hints: You need a branch command that shows both local and remote branches.
Add the -a (all) flag to git branch.
Run `git branch -a`, then look for your feature branch under the lines that start with remotes/.
If your feature branch appears as remotes/origin/<name>, don't rebase it. If it isn't listed there, it is safe to rebase.
common_mistakes: Running plain `git branch` without -a, which hides the remote branches.
Mistaking the local feature branch line for a pushed branch. Only lines starting with remotes/ count.
Relying on a stale view: remote branches pushed by a teammate show up only after `git fetch`.
Running the command outside the repository folder and getting 'fatal: not a git repository'.

steps.title: Set up and start a conflicting
steps.instructions: Create `feature/login` from main with three commits, where the first and third change the same line of `app.txt` that two new main commits also change. On `feature/login`, run `git rebase main` and then `git status` to see the paused rebase.

targets.caption: The rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit
git status shows the paused rebase
Remaining feature commits waiting to be reapplied

explanations.topic: Rebase sets your commits aside, then reapplies them one by one, so each one can conflict
The feature commits branch off an older main commit; rebase makes the newest main commit their new base
Rebase pauses at a conflict; git status shows which commit failed and how many remain
Fixing rebase conflicts works like merge conflicts: remove markers and keep the right code

hints: On main, change one line of app.txt and commit twice. Then branch from the earlier commit so the branch shares the old base.
On feature/login, make three commits: commit 1 edits that same app.txt line, commit 2 edits a different file, commit 3 edits the app.txt line again.
Make sure feature/login is checked out, run `git rebase main`, and then run `git status`.
If the rebase finishes with no conflict, your branch commits did not change the same line that main changed. Run `git rebase --abort` (or reset), make the edits overlap, and retry.
common_mistakes: Creating feature/login from main's latest commit. Main then has nothing new to rebase onto and no conflict appears.
Editing different lines of app.txt on the two branches. Git merges these automatically, so you get no conflict.
Running `git rebase main` while on main instead of on feature/login.
Leaving uncommitted changes in the working tree. Git refuses to start the rebase.
Panicking at the conflict and running `git rebase --abort`. The paused state is the expected result of this step.

steps.title: Resolve the first conflict and continue
steps.instructions: Open the conflicted file, delete the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers keeping the correct code, then run `git add` on it. Run `git rebase --continue` and, in Vim, press Escape and type `:wq` to accept the commit message.

targets.caption: Delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, keeping the correct code
After git add, continue the rebase instead of committing
In Vim: press Escape, type :wq and press Enter

explanations.topic: Stage resolved files with git add
Use git rebase --continue instead of commit during a rebase
Vim opens for the commit message; Escape then :wq saves and closes
Accepting the message leaves the original commit message unchanged

hints: Run git status to see which files are listed under 'both modified'. Those are the ones to fix.
Open each conflicted file and delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line. Keep only the code that should remain.
Run git add <file> for every file you fixed, then run git rebase --continue (don't run git commit).
When Vim opens, press Esc, type :wq and press Enter to accept the existing commit message.
common_mistakes: Leaving a stray ======= or >>>>>>> marker line in the file
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue
Forgetting to git add the resolved file, so git refuses to continue
Getting stuck in Vim by typing :wq without pressing Escape first
Deleting both versions of the conflicting code instead of keeping the correct one

steps.title: Finish the rebase
steps.instructions: Fix the conflict from the third commit the same way, git add the file and run git rebase --continue again. Run git status to confirm you are no longer rebasing.

precision_checks.label: No rebase in progress
precision_checks.command: test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge)" && test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-apply)"

targets.caption: The final git rebase --continue finishes the rebase
git status no longer reports a rebase in progress

explanations.topic: Non-conflicting commits are applied automatically during a rebase
Git pauses again at each conflicting commit
Using git status to confirm the rebase is finished

hints: Git applies commits one at a time. It stops only at commits that conflict. Run git status to see which file is conflicted now.
Open the conflicted file. Remove the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers, keeping the content you want. Then save the file.
Run git add <file> and then git rebase --continue. Save and close the commit-message editor to accept the message.
Run git status at the end. It should say 'On branch ...' and should not mention a rebase in progress.
common_mistakes: Leaving conflict markers in the file before running git add.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue, or forgetting to continue after git add.
Not closing the commit-message editor, so the rebase seems stuck.
Running git rebase --skip by accident, which drops the third commit.
Assuming the rebase finished after the first conflict, when it still has to pause at the third commit.
steps.code:
git add <conflicting-file>
git rebase --continue
git status
